NEW YORK (CNN) -- She survived a bloodbath at a Lane Bryant store in Tinley Park, Illinois, by playing dead. The only survivor, she gave police a detailed description of the gunman. The Illinois State police worked closely with the survivor to come up with a composite of the gunman. Police aren't identifying their witness to protect her safety. The crime began to unfold shortly after 10 a.m. when a man posing as a delivery man walked into the store. He chatted briefly with two customers and two employees. Then, police said, he pulled out a gun and announced a holdup. He forced the four women into the back room, police said. He bound them with duct tape and placed them face down on the floor. Two more women who later entered the store also were taken to the back room, tied and placed next to the others.  Watch an update on the case » . Store manager Rhoda McFarland managed to call 911 from her cell phone at 10:44 a.m., just before she was shot to death. She got to her phone while the gunman was distracted, even though she was bound by the duct tape. On the call, posted on the Tinley Park police Web site, a man can be heard saying, "I'm losing it." The six women were shot execution style. Five of them were dead by the time police arrived, a few minutes after McFarland's call. A sixth woman survived. She, too, had been shot and left for dead, but tricked the killer by pretending to be dead. The killer was not wearing a mask or disguise, so she was able to describe him in detail. She told police he was a 6 foot African-American male, average weight, medium to dark skin tone, with braided hair and cornrows, husky build, and between 25 and 35 years old. His hair was pulled back, but one braid hung along his right cheek with light-green beads at the end of it, she told police. Police have released a composite sketch based on the witness' description. Besides store manager McFarland, the other women slain were Jennifer Bishop, Connie Woolfolk, Carrie Hudek Chiuso and Sarah Szafranski. The investigation remains open and active, and all theories are still being investigated, police say. The investigation has included a thorough vetting of the victims' backgrounds to determine whether any of them had any enemies. "None of the victimology so far has led to any suspects yet," said Commander Pat McCain of the Tinley Park Police Department. Police aren't ruling out any theories, including robbery. The gunman took a few hundred dollars, police said. "Certainly, the surviving witness didn't seem to recognize the killer, but maybe one of the dead victims knew him. We don't know," McCain said. The weapon used was a .40-caliber Glock. Bullet casings were left at the scene and the killer took the weapon with him. More than a year later, forensics from the crime scene are still being processed, police said. Investigators won't comment on whether the gunman left any fingerprints, hair or other trace evidence. Police say they have received more than 5,000 tips and feel this case will be solved. But at this point, they have not named a person of interest or a suspect. Investigators are asking for the public's help. There is a $100,000 reward for the arrest of the person or persons responsible for the Lane Bryant shootings. Have information? NEW YORK (CNN) -- By feigning death, one woman managed to escape a massacre that claimed five lives at a Lane Bryant clothing store in Tinley Park, Illinois. As the lone survivor, she provided investigators with a thorough physical description of the shooter, which the Illinois State Police used to develop a composite sketch. To keep her safe, authorities are withholding her identity.

The tragedy occurred on February 2, 2008, when a suspect—still unidentified today—entered the store around 10 a.m. disguised as a delivery worker. After briefly making conversation with two shoppers and two staff members, he drew a firearm and declared a robbery underway.

The four women were herded into a back room, where he restrained them with duct tape and forced them to lie face-down. Two additional customers who arrived afterward met the same fate, bound and placed alongside the others.

Amid the chaos, store manager Rhoda McFarland managed a brief window of opportunity while the gunman's attention lapsed—despite being taped up, she reached her cell phone and dialed 911 at 10:44 a.m. Moments later, she was fatally shot. A recording of that call, now available on the Tinley Park police website, captures the assailant muttering, "I'm losing it."

All six victims were shot in what authorities describe as an execution-style attack. By the time officers arrived—mere minutes after McFarland's call—five women had already died. The sixth victim, though also shot and presumed dead by the attacker, survived by successfully playing dead.

Because the perpetrator wore no mask, the surviving witness could offer specific details about his appearance. According to her account, he stood approximately six feet tall, was African-American with a medium-to-dark complexion, had a stocky build, and appeared to be somewhere between 25 and 35 years old. His hair was styled in cornrows and braids pulled back from his face, with one braid falling along his right cheek, decorated with light-green beads at its tip. This description formed the basis for the composite sketch police subsequently released.

The victims who lost their lives, aside from McFarland, were identified as Jennifer Bishop, Connie Woolfolk, Carrie Hudek Chiuso, and Sarah Szafranski.

Authorities describe the case as still open, with investigators pursuing every possible angle. This has included a comprehensive review of each victim's personal history to identify potential enemies or connections to the killer. "None of the victimology so far has led to any suspects yet," noted Commander Pat McCain of the Tinley Park Police Department.

Robbery hasn't been eliminated as a motive—the gunman fled with only a few hundred dollars. McCain acknowledged the puzzling nature of the case: "Certainly, the surviving witness didn't seem to recognize the killer, but maybe one of the dead victims knew him. We don't know."

Ballistic evidence recovered from the scene identified the weapon as a .40-caliber Glock; while spent casings were left behind, the gun itself was taken by the killer. Even now, more than a year after the shooting, forensic analysis from the crime scene continues, though police have declined to reveal whether fingerprints, hair samples, or other physical evidence were recovered.

Despite receiving over 5,000 tips from the public, investigators have yet to name a suspect or person of interest. Nevertheless, they remain optimistic about eventually solving the case and continue to seek public assistance.

A $100,000 reward is being offered for information leading to the arrest of whoever committed the Lane Bryant shootings. Anyone with relevant information is urged to contact the Tinley Park Police tip line at (708) 444-5394 or submit tips through the department's website.

*Tinley Park, Illinois (CNN)* — Investigators are searching for a gunman who opened fire inside a Lane Bryant clothing store in this southwest Chicago suburb, killing five women in what authorities are calling one of the most disturbing crimes in the area's history.

The shooting occurred February 2 at the store, located in a strip mall along 191st Street, just before the business was scheduled to open to the public. Police say the gunman entered during a time when only employees and a few customers were inside, ordered the women into a back stockroom, and then shot each of them at close range.

Killed in the attack were store manager Rhoda McFarland, 42; employees Sarah Szafranski, 22, and Carrie Chiuso, 33; along with customers Jennifer Bishop, 34, and Connie Woolfolk, 37. All five died at the scene or shortly after being taken to area hospitals.

**A Survivor's Call for Help**

One woman survived the shooting despite being wounded, and her actions in its immediate aftermath have become a critical piece of the investigation. Officials say the woman, whose identity has been withheld at her family's request, was shot but managed to remain conscious. After the gunman left the store, she crawled to a phone and called 911, providing dispatchers with a description of the shooter and details about the vehicle he was seen driving away in.

"Her composure and presence of mind under the most horrific circumstances gave investigators a head start we might not otherwise have had," a Tinley Park police spokesperson said. Authorities credit her account with generating an early composite sketch of the suspect, described as a white or Hispanic man in his 20s or 30s.

The survivor was hospitalized for her injuries and, according to family members, is expected to recover physically, though relatives say she continues to struggle emotionally with having lost coworkers and a customer in the attack.

**A Community in Shock**

News of the shooting stunned Tinley Park, a quiet suburb of roughly 55,000 residents not accustomed to violent crime. Shoppers left flowers and stuffed animals outside the shuttered storefront in the days following the attack, and vigils were held at local churches.

"This is not something that happens here," said one longtime resident who lives near the shopping center. "Everybody knows somebody who shopped at that store."

Lane Bryant's parent company, Charming Shoppes, closed the location indefinitely and offered counseling services to employees at other area stores.

**The Investigation**

The Cook County Sheriff's Office and Tinley Park police, working alongside the FBI, have assembled a task force to pursue leads in the case. Investigators have not released a motive and have said robbery does not appear to have been the primary aim, as store cash and merchandise were reportedly left untouched.

Forensic teams processed the scene extensively, and officials say DNA evidence recovered from the store is being analyzed at a state crime lab. Police have also released the composite sketch derived from witness accounts, along with a description of the suspect's vehicle, believed to be a dark-colored SUV.

A tip line has been established, and a reward — reported to be in excess of $50,000 and growing as community organizations and businesses contribute — has been offered for information leading to an arrest.

"We are pursuing every lead, no matter how small," said a spokesperson for the joint task force. "We will not rest until the person responsible for this is behind bars."

As of this week, no arrests have been made, and police have urged residents in the region to remain vigilant while the investigation continues.

*CNN will continue to follow developments in this case.*

Her survival and willingness to cooperate with investigators despite the trauma provided law enforcement with the only firsthand account of what transpired inside that back room—information that has remained a cornerstone of the case for over a decade.

## The Investigation

The case immediately drew massive attention from local and federal law enforcement, including the FBI, given the brutality and randomness of the attack. Investigators pursued thousands of leads over the years, DNA evidence was collected from the scene, and the composite sketch was widely circulated.

Despite these efforts, no arrest was made for years. The case went cold, frustrating both investigators and the victims' families who continued to publicly advocate for renewed attention to the case.

## Breakthrough and Resolution

In 2019, more than a decade after the killings, investigators announced a break in the case. **Charles Jason Cooke** was named as a suspect, tied to the crime through DNA evidence recovered from the scene. Cooke, however, was already deceased—he had died in 2015 from other causes, reportedly related to a leukemia diagnosis.

The revelation brought a form of resolution to the families of the victims, though not the traditional justice of a trial and conviction. Prosecutors and investigators expressed confidence in the DNA match, effectively closing the case despite the absence of a living defendant to prosecute.

## Legacy

The Lane Bryant killings remain etched in the memory of the Chicago suburbs as a stark reminder of random violence's capacity to shatter an ordinary day. The survivor's courage in providing testimony under unimaginable circumstances, combined with persistent forensic work over eleven years, eventually pieced together an answer—even if it came too late for a courtroom reckoning.

The case underscores both the limitations and eventual power of DNA technology in solving crimes that might otherwise remain permanently unsolved, offering some measure of closure to a community that spent over a decade seeking answers.
